questions.question: What is 'confidence signaling' in AI UX design?
options: Making all AI responses look identical regardless of their reliability
Visually distinguishing higher-confidence or grounded output (e.g. with citations) from lower-confidence or unverified output
A technique for making a model generate faster
A backend-only concept with no effect on the user interface
questions.explanation: Confidence signaling gives users visual cues (like citations or warning badges) to calibrate how much to trust a given AI response, rather than presenting every output with the same unearned authority.

questions.question: Why does presenting every AI response with uniform, unqualified confidence tend to backfire?
options: It doesn't backfire — uniform presentation is always the best approach
It sets users up to trust wrong answers exactly as much as right ones, so trust erodes suddenly and severely once a mistake is discovered, rather than being managed gradually and honestly
Users always ignore AI-generated content regardless of presentation
This only matters for image-generation features, not text
questions.explanation: Without confidence signaling, users have no basis to be more skeptical of lower-confidence outputs, so when a mistake surfaces, it damages trust more severely than if uncertainty had been honestly communicated all along.

questions.question: An AI feature is rate-limited and the UI simply shows a blank or broken-looking response with no explanation. Which question best addresses this UX gap?
options: Should we just accept this as an unavoidable limitation?
Does our UI clearly communicate degraded states (like rate limiting) to users, or does it present a silently broken experience with no explanation?
Should we remove rate limiting entirely to avoid this issue?
Is this purely a backend engineering problem with no UX component?
questions.explanation: This is a graceful degradation gap — the fix is ensuring degraded states are clearly communicated to users (e.g. 'high demand, please try again') rather than presenting an unexplained broken experience.
